claims.text: HEA coatings on transition-metal matrices initially improve in tribological performance as ambient temperature increases moderately, up to about 300°C.
The proposed moderate-temperature improvement is caused by formation of a protective tribo-oxide layer that reduces friction and wear.
Tribological performance degrades significantly beyond a critical temperature of approximately 300–400°C.
Excessive tribochemical reactions at elevated temperature increase friction in CuMoTaWV sliding against a steel counterface.
Above the proposed threshold, instability of the oxide layer causes rapid wear.
Above the proposed threshold, increased adhesion and plastic deformation drastically increase friction and wear.
The example initial state is a nanocrystalline CuMoTaWV refractory HEA coating deposited on a 304 stainless-steel substrate.
The CuMoTaWV coating has an average grain size of approximately 18 nm and hardness of approximately 19 GPa.
The CuMoTaWV coating was tested in sliding against E52100 alloy steel under a 1 N load.
The relevant test conditions include an atmospheric environment and test temperatures from room temperature to 300°C.
The cited CuMoTaWV tests include tribological measurements above 300°C.
The temperature-dependent structural mediator includes formation of CuO, MoO3, and WO3 in the tribo-oxide layer.
Surface roughness and coating adhesion affect the wear behavior of the CuMoTaWV coating.
A stable oxide layer acts as a solid lubricant at moderate temperature.
Wear rate and coefficient of friction have a minimum near 300°C.
For CuMoTaWV, the coefficient of friction rises from approximately 0.25 at room temperature to approximately 1.5 at 300°C.
For CuMoTaWV, the wear rate rises from approximately 6.4 × 10^-6 mm³/(N·m) at room temperature to approximately 2.5 × 10^-5 mm³/(N·m) at 300°C.
The relatively low room-temperature friction and wear of the annealed coating are associated with high hardness, nanocrystallinity, and improved adhesion.
Above 300°C, wear rate and coefficient of friction increase sharply.
The degradation boundary is approximately 300–400°C.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says performance improves with temperature up to about 300°C, but the quantified prediction reports both COF and wear rate increasing substantially from room temperature to 300°C.

The claimed minimum in COF and wear rate near 300°C is incompatible with the stated CuMoTaWV values: COF increases from 0.25 to 1.5 and wear rate increases from 6.4 × 10^-6 to 2.5 × 10^-5 mm³/(N·m) between room temperature and 300°C.

The mechanism describes the oxide layer at moderate temperatures up to roughly 300°C as protective and friction-reducing, whereas the same-system prediction and evidence attribute the high COF at 300°C to tribochemical reactions and oxide formation.
